title: Arrays and Strings
subtitle: Arrays and Strings: build, inspect, test, and apply the concept
description: An interactive, dashboard-focused lesson on arrays and strings, with worked code, deliberate debugging, practical transfer, and five explained application questions.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Arrays and Strings: foundations and mental model

Arrays and Strings is not just a syntax topic: it is a way to make the application’s intent explicit. Choose sequences for ordered items and maps for keyed lookup. Validate indexes and missing keys; empty collections must have deliberate behavior. In the Code Academy dashboard, that idea matters because A score tracker makes explicit types, array bounds, and pointer validity important. Start by identifying the input, the rule being applied, and the result that a learner should observe. Separate what the code declares from what it actually does at runtime. A name, selector, function, condition, or query should express one clear responsibility. When reading an example, predict its behavior before running or reviewing the output. If the prediction is wrong, trace each meaningful line instead of rewriting everything at once. This habit builds the kind of reasoning that transfers to unfamiliar code, not merely a memory of one sample. The first example introduces the smallest useful version of the idea; later examples test it against variations and edge cases.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Arrays and Strings: The first array item has index zero
blocks.output: The first array item has index zero.

blocks.text: Example 1 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “int scores[] = {3, 5, 2};”: Declares or assigns a value. The name and type determine how later expressions can use it. Line 2 — “printf("%d\n", scores[0]);”: Continues the example’s expression or control block. Read it in order with the preceding declaration and following result. Expected behavior: The first array item has index zero. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A course list contains three entries and uses zero-based indexing. Which expression selects the first item?
options: courses[3]
courses[-3] in every language
courses[0]
courses[1]
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: courses[0]. In zero-based arrays, index zero refers to the first entry.
blocks.reasoning: In zero-based arrays, index zero refers to the first entry. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Arrays and Strings: Computes the number of elements

blocks.text: Example 2 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “int scores[] = {3, 5, 2};”: Declares or assigns a value. The name and type determine how later expressions can use it. Line 2 — “size_t count = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);”: Assigns or updates state; later lines observe the new value, so the right-hand expression matters. Line 3 — “printf("%zu scores\n", count);”: Continues the example’s expression or control block. Read it in order with the preceding declaration and following result. Expected behavior: Computes the number of elements. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: The dashboard must prevent the same completed lesson ID being counted twice. Which data structure is a natural fit?
options: A counter incremented without checking the lesson ID
A set or a keyed map that enforces unique IDs
An unparsed text string with duplicates
Parallel arrays with no shared key
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: A set or a keyed map that enforces unique IDs. Uniqueness should be enforced by the data structure or explicit key check.
blocks.reasoning: Uniqueness should be enforced by the data structure or explicit key check. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Arrays and Strings: implementation, debugging, and edge cases

Implementation quality depends on details that are easy to miss. Choose sequences for ordered items and maps for keyed lookup. Validate indexes and missing keys; empty collections must have deliberate behavior. Compare the expected result with the actual result, then ask which smallest change explains any difference. Check the data type, boundaries, execution order, and assumptions about missing or invalid input. For the Code Academy dashboard, A score tracker makes explicit types, array bounds, and pointer validity important. A solution that works only for one perfect input is incomplete. For instance, check empty strings, a zero count, an unavailable resource, an unknown key, or a repeated user action whenever those cases fit the feature. Keep responsibilities small so the cause of a defect can be isolated. The second and third examples show how to make the logic clearer and how to recognize a failure mode. Read the comments and output notes as a guide to reasoning, not as a substitute for inspecting every statement.

blocks.title: Example 3 — Arrays and Strings: A character array stores a null-terminated string
blocks.output: A character array stores a null-terminated string.

Line 2 — “printf("%s\n", course);”: Continues the example’s expression or control block. Read it in order with the preceding declaration and following result. Expected behavior: A character array stores a null-terminated string. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A dictionary lookup may not find a key. What should the code do?
options: Handle the missing-key result or use a deliberate fallback
Assume the lookup always succeeds
Treat the key’s absence as proof that its value is zero
Access a missing nested property without checking
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Handle the missing-key result or use a deliberate fallback. A missing key may be distinct from a key whose value is zero or empty.
blocks.reasoning: A missing key may be distinct from a key whose value is zero or empty. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 4 — Arrays and Strings: Counts truth-like integer flags

blocks.text: Example 4 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “int completed[] = {1, 1, 0};”: Declares or assigns a value. The name and type determine how later expressions can use it. Line 2 — “int count = 0;”: Declares or assigns a value. The name and type determine how later expressions can use it. Line 3 — “for (int i=0; i<3; i++) count += completed[i];”: Repeats an operation over a sequence or while a condition is met; its bounds and update control termination. Line 4 — “printf("%d completed\n", count);”: Continues the example’s expression or control block. Read it in order with the preceding declaration and following result. Expected behavior: Counts truth-like integer flags. What if a line changes? If the loop update or stopping condition is removed or changed, iterations may be skipped, repeated, or never finish. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: Each quiz attempt has both correctness and XP. Which representation best preserves the relationship?
options: Separate arrays that can become different lengths
One string containing all values without delimiters
A single number containing the sum only
A list of structured attempt records
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: A list of structured attempt records. Records keep related fields together and prevent losing which XP belongs to which attempt.
blocks.reasoning: Records keep related fields together and prevent losing which XP belongs to which attempt. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Arrays and Strings: applied challenge and mastery check

Professional practice means verifying the requirement from a learner’s point of view. Choose sequences for ordered items and maps for keyed lookup. Validate indexes and missing keys; empty collections must have deliberate behavior. For the Code Academy dashboard, A score tracker makes explicit types, array bounds, and pointer validity important. Finish by following a small test sequence: verify a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case; confirm the page remains understandable; and check that the result matches the requirement rather than merely appearing plausible. Ask what would happen if one important line were removed, changed, or called in the wrong order. Distinguish a syntax error from a logic error and from an interface or data issue. The final sample brings the concept into a compact applied task, and the questions ask for decisions rather than isolated definitions. A strong answer should be supported by a reason and by a test that could prove or disprove the assumption.

Applied challenge: implement a small Code Academy feature that uses arrays and strings. Define the expected behavior in one sentence, identify the input and output, and choose the simplest code pattern above that fits. Test a normal case and an edge case. Then make one controlled change: remove a condition, alter a value, or change an input shape. Record what breaks and explain why. This is the “do and let me do” part of the lesson: the concept becomes memorable when the learner predicts a result, observes it, and explains the difference.

blocks.question: A score array may be empty. What should the maximum-score calculation consider?
options: Use the array length as the maximum score
Sort it and read index zero without a check
Handle the empty collection before assuming a maximum exists
Assume the maximum is always the first item
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Handle the empty collection before assuming a maximum exists. An empty collection has no element to return as its maximum.
blocks.reasoning: An empty collection has no element to return as its maximum. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: Lesson recap: Choose sequences for ordered items and maps for keyed lookup. Validate indexes and missing keys; empty collections must have deliberate behavior. Keep the underlying rule in mind when moving to more complex dashboard features. Syntax is the visible surface; reliable reasoning, validation, and testing are the transferable skill.
